question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{3}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{30}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}\begin{bmatrix}-2\sqrt{5} \\ -\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,-2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{(-1)}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\frac{2}{5}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 & \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{15}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{15}}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5} \\ -\sqrt{5}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}

Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{4}{5}{x}_{1}+\frac{3}{5}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,4{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{4} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{5} & -\frac{3}{5} & 0 \\ \frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=4$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,\,-2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{1} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=0.7x-0.35xy \\ {y}^{′} &=-0.4y+2xy\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0.2,\,2]^{T},$ we get
$J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}{{field-4}}
$\,.$
$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are {{field-5}}. $\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is {{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=0.7x-0.35xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-0.4y+2xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(0.7x-0.35xy)=0.7-0.35y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(0.7x-0.35xy)=-0.35x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-0.4y+2xy)=2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-0.4y+2xy)=-0.4+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}0.7-0.35y & -0.35x \\ 2y & -0.4+2x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0.2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}0.7-0.35(2) & -0.35(0.2) \\ 2(2) & -0.4+2(0.2)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -0.07 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-\lambda  & -0.07 \\ 4 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-\lambda )-4\cdot (-0.07) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.28 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=\pm 0.2\sqrt{7}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is $\text{a stable}$ $\text{center}.$

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model (as in this problem), it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues. 

**Watch out!** 
In contrast, for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone is inconclusive (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source).

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=x(1-x)-xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-y+2xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x(1-x)-xy)=1-2x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x(1-x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-y+2xy)=2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y+2xy)=-1+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}1-2x-y & -x \\ 2y & -1+2x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0.5 \\ 0.5\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}1-2(0.5)-0.5 & -0.5 \\ 2(0.5) & -1+2(0.5)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.5 & -0.5 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-0.5-\lambda  & -0.5 \\ 1 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-0.5-\lambda )(-\lambda )-1(-0.5) & =0 \\ \lambda (0.5+\lambda )+0.5 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.5\lambda +0.5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-0.25\pm 0.25\sqrt{7}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are complex with negative real parts, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ $\text{spiral sink}.$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=4x(1-2x)-xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-3y+3xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x(1-2x)-xy)=4-16x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x(1-2x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y+3xy)=3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y+3xy)=-3+3x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}4-16x-y & -x \\ 3y & -3+3x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}4-16(0)-0 & -0 \\ 3(0) & -3+3(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=-0.5x+0.5xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=y-5xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-0.5x+0.5xy)=-0.5+0.5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-0.5x+0.5xy)=0.5x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-5xy)=-5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-5xy)=1-5x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}-0.5+0.5y & 0.5x \\ -5y & 1-5x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium $$
\displaystyle {x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0.2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}-0.5+0.5(1) & 0.5(0.2) \\ -5(1) & 1-5(0.2)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0.1 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-\lambda  & 0.1 \\ -5 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-\lambda )-(-5)\cdot 0.1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=\pm 0.5\sqrt{2}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is $\text{a stable}$ $\text{center}.$

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model (as in this problem), it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues. 

**Watch out!** 
In contrast, for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone is inconclusive (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source).

Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=2x(1-0.25x)-xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-3y+xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x(1-0.25x)-xy)=2-x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x(1-0.25x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y+xy)=y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y+xy)=-3+x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}2-x-y & -x \\ y & -3+x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2-4-0 & -4 \\ 0 & -3+4\end{bmatrix}\,\,=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=1\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$

question.:question/problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}x+\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,x(1)=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} $$ Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above. *Hint: $$ \displaystyle {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}, $$ where $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}. $$*
$x(t)=\,\,$
$2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(5(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5(t-1))$
{{field-2}}
$\displaystyle \,\,+{\int }_{1}^{t}\,\,$
{{field-1}}
${e}^{5s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5(t-s))$
$\,\,\text{d}s$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that $$
\displaystyle {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(5(t-1)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(5(t-1)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(5(t-1)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(5(t-1))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(5(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5(t-1)) \\ 2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5(t-1))+\operatorname{cosh}⁡(5(t-1))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(5(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(5(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(5(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(5(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(5(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(5(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(5(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(5(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5s} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(5(t-s)) \\ {e}^{5s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(5(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5(t-1)) \\ 2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5(t-1))+\operatorname{cosh}⁡(5(t-1))\end{bmatrix}+{\int }_{1}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(5(t-s)) \\ {e}^{5s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(5(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{s} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(t-s) \\ {e}^{s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(t)+2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t)+2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(t)\end{bmatrix}+{\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(t-s) \\ {e}^{s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Solving an Inhomogeneous System Using a Given Matrix Exponential

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=4x(t)+4,\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*
$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\,\,$
{{field-1}}
$\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.
$\displaystyle \operatorname{sin}⁡\left({J}_{4}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\right)=\frac{1}{12}\,\,$

$0$$0$$6${{field-4}}
$0$$0$$0$$6$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ $n=4,$ and $\lambda =\frac{\pi }{6}.$

Since $n=4,$ we need to compute the first $4-1=3$ derivatives of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f\left({J}_{4}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\right) & =\begin{bmatrix}f\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) & {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) & \frac{1}{3!}{f}^{‴}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\ 0 & f\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) & {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\ 0 & 0 & f\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) & {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & f\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) & \operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) & -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) & -\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\ 0 & \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) & \operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) & -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) & \operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{12} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 6\sqrt{3} & -3 & -\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 6 & 6\sqrt{3} & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 & 6\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Solving an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs Using Variation of Parameters

question.:question/problem:
$$ \mathbf{x}'(t) = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}- 2 & 0 \\ 0 & - 4\end{array} \right]} \mathbf{x}(t) + {\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 t \\ 0\end{array} \right]} $$ Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form
$\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 0\end{array} \right]} e^{-2t} + c_2{\left[ \begin{array}{c}0 \\ 1\end{array} \right]} e^{-4t} +\:\:$
$\boxed{\rule{0pt}{1.3em}\phantom{xxxxxxxx}}$
$0$
$.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{x}_c(t) + \mathbf{x}_p(t)
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_c(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that
$$
\mathbf{x}_c(t) = c_1{\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 0\end{array} \right]} e^{-2t} + c_2{\left[ \begin{array}{c}0 \\ 1\end{array} \right]} e^{-4t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \, \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

In our case,
$$
\Phi = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{e}^{- 2 t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{- 4 t}\end{array} \right]}, \qquad
\mathbf{f}(t) = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 t \\ 0\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{-4t}-0}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{6t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2t{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $\mathbf{u}(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}2t{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int 2t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 0\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=2t$ and $\text{d}v=e^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=2\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(2\,\text{d}t) \\  & =t{e}^{2t}-\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(2t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, the integrand is zero, so the integral is zero.

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(2t-1) \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2t-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Particular Solution of an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations: $$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} $$ The complementary solution to this system is given by $$ {x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R. $$ Then, the general solution of the system is
$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+$ {{field-1}} $\cdot \,\,$
$0$
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is exponential. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also exponential, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $a,b$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=-2{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot {e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}+{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\ -2\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-2a \\ -2b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-b \\ 4a\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-2a \\ -2b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-b+1 \\ 4a-2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-b+1 &=-2a \\ 4a-2 &=-2b\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we get 

$$
b=2a+1.
$$

 
Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $b,$ we have

$$
4a-2=-2(2a+1)\,⇒\,a=0.
$$

So, 

$$
b=2(0)+1=1.
$$

 

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:

Using the method of variation of parameters, compute ${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)$ and the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t)$ of the system.

{{field-1}}
$\,,\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=\,\,$
$2$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{2t}\cdot 2{e}^{4t}-(-3{e}^{4t})\cdot 0}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{4t} & 3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-6t}}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{4t} & 3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & 3{e}^{-2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix} \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & 3{e}^{-2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-10{e}^{-2t} \\ -4{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-10{e}^{-2t} \\ -4{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -10{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -4{e}^{-4t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 3 & -4\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix}6t \\ 3t\end{bmatrix} $$ Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form
$x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+\,\,\frac{1}{4}$
$36t-42$
{{field-1}}
$.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-t} \\ 3{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}6t \\ 3t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t}\cdot 3{e}^{-2t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-{e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}6t \\ 3t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3t{e}^{2t} \\ 12t{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-3t{e}^{2t} \\ 12t{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -3t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 12t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=-3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-3\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -3t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(-3t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (-3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{3}{2}\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{3}{4}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{e}^{2t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=12t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=12\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 12t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =12t\cdot {e}^{t}-\int 12\cdot {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =12t{e}^{t}-12{e}^{t} \\  & =12{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-t} \\ 3{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{4}{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\ 12{e}^{t}(t-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}6(1-2t)+48(t-1) \\ 9(1-2t)+48(t-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}36t-42 \\ 30t-39\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing Two Iterations of the Newton-Raphson Method

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[1,2]\times [1,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}y+x-3 \\ x{y}^{2}-y-1\end{bmatrix}. $$ Calculate the second iteration of the Newton-Raphson process that starts at ${x}_{0}=[1,\,1]^{T}$ if the first iteration of the algorithm gives ${x}_{1}=[1,\,2]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
${x}_{2}\,≈$
$1.091$
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y+x-3) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y+x-3) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-y-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-y-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2xy+1 & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy-1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}2xy+1 & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy-1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}y+x-3 \\ x{y}^{2}-y-1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
{H}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-∇f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(5{x}^{2}y-4x+2{y}^{3}-6{y}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(5{x}^{2}y-4x+2{y}^{3}-6{y}^{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}10xy-4 \\ 5{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}-12y\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(10xy-4) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(5{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}-12y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(10xy-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(5{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}-12y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}10y & 10x \\ 10x & 12y-12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}10y & 10x \\ 10x & 12y-12\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}10xy-4 \\ 5{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}-12y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}10y & 10x \\ 10x & 12y-12\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}10xy-4 \\ 5{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}-12y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}10(1) & 10(1) \\ 10(1) & 12(1)-12\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}10(1)(1)-4 \\ 5(1)^{2}+6(1)^{2}-12(1)\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}10 & 10 \\ 10 & 0\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Applying the Chain Rule to Calculate Gradients

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{2\times 3}\to R$ defined by $L(A)=\frac{1}{2}(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b),$ where $$ x=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 10 \\ 20\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}? $$
${∇}_{A}=\,\,$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
$0${{field-4}}$-160$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of $L$ with respect to $A$ is a matrix of the same shape as $A$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=Ax-b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}\left(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y\right)=y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}={y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=Ax-b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}={\sum }_{j=1}^{3}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-{b}_{i},
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}={x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}{x}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{A}L & =y\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =(Ax-b)\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =\left(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 10 \\ 20\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 10 & 20\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\left(\begin{bmatrix}20 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 10 & 20\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}13 \\ -8\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 10 & 20\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 130 & 260 \\ 0 & -80 & -160\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix},
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix},
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 3 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $$
\displaystyle x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}:
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 3 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2+0 \\ 3+0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that to find a unit vector that is parallel to a given vector, we need to divide the given vector by its length:

$$
u=\frac{v}{|\,v\,|}
$$

Using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,v\,| & =\sqrt{{v}_{x}^{2}+{v}_{y}^{2}+{v}_{z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+0+4} \\  & =\sqrt{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide $v$ by its length and get the following unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{v}{|\,v\,|} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}v \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{8}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{8}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)={3}^{x},$ $n=2,$ and $\lambda =1.$

Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first $2-1=1$ derivatives of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={3}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={3}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(1)) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & f(1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{3}^{1} & {3}^{1}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ 0 & {3}^{1}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2({J}_{3}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2))} & ={3}^{\left(\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{3}(1) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{1}(2)\end{bmatrix}\right)} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{3}^{({J}_{3}(1))} & 0 \\ 0 & {3}^{({J}_{1}(2))}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={3}^{({J}_{3}(1))}\,⊕\,{3}^{({J}_{1}(2))}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{3}(1),$ we have $n=3$ and $\lambda =2.$ Since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first and second derivative of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={3}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={3}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={3}^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(1)) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(1) \\ 0 & f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & 0 & f(1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{3}^{1} & {3}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & \frac{1}{2}\cdot {3}^{1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡3)^{2} \\ 0 & {3}^{1} & {3}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ 0 & 0 & {3}^{1}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & \frac{3}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡3)^{2} \\ 0 & 3 & 3\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{1}(2),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =1.$ since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(2)) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{3}^{(2)}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{({J}_{3}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2))} & ={3}^{({J}_{3}(1))}\,⊕\,{3}^{({J}_{1}(2))} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & \frac{3}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡3)^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 3\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as

$$
{J}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2xy-{y}^{2}+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2xy-{y}^{2}+1) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-x+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-x+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x+2y & 2x-2y \\ {y}^{2}-1 & 2xy\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
The second-order differential equation ${y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+3y={e}^{t}$ can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ where
$x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,A=\,\,$

and for $y=y(t),$ we have $y={x}_{1}(t)$ and ${y}^{′}={x}_{2}(t).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=2{y}^{′}-3y+{e}^{t}.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=2{x}_{2}-3{x}_{1}+{e}^{t}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &=-3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Particular Solution of an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations: $$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+{e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}. $$ The complementary solution to this system is given by $$ {x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R. $$ Then, the general solution of the system is
$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+$ {{field-1}} $\cdot \,\,$
$-\frac{7}{10}$
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
{e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is exponential. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also exponential, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $a,b$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=-{e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot {e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}+{e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ -\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-a \\ -b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3b \\ 3a\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-a \\ -b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3b+4 \\ 3a+1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3b+4 &=-a \\ 3a+1 &=-b\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we get 

$$
a=3b-4.
$$

 
Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $b,$ we have

$$
3(3b-4)+1=-b\,⇒\,b=\frac{11}{10}.
$$

So, 

$$
a=3\cdot \frac{11}{10}-4=\frac{33}{10}-\frac{40}{10}=-\frac{7}{10}.
$$

 

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{7}{10} \\ \frac{11}{10}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
\begin{bmatrix}t-3 \\ 2t+1\end{bmatrix}
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix},
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2}$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-1/2 & 3/2 \\ 3/2 & -1/2\end{bmatrix}\left(\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\right)+\begin{bmatrix}t-3 \\ 2t+1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}({a}_{1}t+{b}_{1})+\frac{3}{2}({a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}) \\ \frac{3}{2}({a}_{1}t+{b}_{1})-\frac{1}{2}({a}_{2}t+{b}_{2})\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}t-3 \\ 2t+1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0t+{a}_{1} \\ 0t+{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}\left(-\frac{{a}_{1}}{2}+\frac{3{a}_{2}}{2}+1\right)t+\left(-\frac{{b}_{1}}{2}+\frac{3{b}_{2}}{2}-3\right) \\ \left(\frac{3{a}_{1}}{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}}{2}+2\right)t+\left(\frac{3{b}_{1}}{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}}{2}+1\right)\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{{a}_{1}}{2}+\frac{3{a}_{2}}{2}+1 &=0 \\ \frac{3{a}_{1}}{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}}{2}+2 &=0 \\ -\frac{{b}_{1}}{2}+\frac{3{b}_{2}}{2}-3 &={a}_{1} \\ \frac{3{b}_{1}}{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}}{2}+1 &={a}_{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first two equations, we get 

$$
{a}_{1}=-\frac{7}{4},\,{a}_{2}=-\frac{5}{4}.
$$

 
Substituting these into the third and fourth equations, and solving for ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2},$ we have

$$
{b}_{1}=-\frac{11}{8},\,{b}_{2}=\frac{3}{8}.
$$

 

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{7}{4} \\ -\frac{5}{4}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{11}{8} \\ \frac{3}{8}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Real Eigenvalues

question.:question/problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}-5 & -6 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}.$ *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $-2$ and $1.$*
${e}^{At}=\,\,$
$-{e}^{t}+2{e}^{-2t}$$-2{e}^{t}+2{e}^{-2t}$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Explanation:

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-5 & -6 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-2t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-2t) &={e}^{-2t} \\ r(t) &={e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-2t} \\ t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-3t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}-{e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{-2t}-{e}^{t}).
$$

- Multiplying the second equation by $2$ and adding to the first one, we get

$$
3{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}+2{e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{3}({e}^{-2t}+2{e}^{t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\alpha }_{1}t & =3\left(-\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{-2t}-{e}^{t})\right)t \\  & =-({e}^{-2t}-{e}^{t}) \\  & ={e}^{t}-{e}^{-2t} \\ 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\left(-\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{-2t}-{e}^{t})\right)t+\frac{1}{3}({e}^{-2t}+2{e}^{t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}((-4{e}^{-2t}+4{e}^{t})+({e}^{-2t}+2{e}^{t})) \\  & =2{e}^{t}-{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{t}+2{e}^{-2t} & -2{e}^{t}+2{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{t}-{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{t}-{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Complex Eigenvalues

question.:question/problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 8 \\ -4 & -3\end{bmatrix}.$ *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $1\pm 4\text{i}.$*
${e}^{At}={e}^{t}\,\,$
$\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$$2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 8 \\ -4 & -3\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 8{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -4{\alpha }_{1}t & -3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=(1+4\text{i})t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=(1-4\text{i})t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((1+4\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(1+4\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(1+4\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ ({\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0})+4{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & ={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\,{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ 4t{\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{4t}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\right)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5\cdot \frac{1}{4t}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\cdot t+{e}^{t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\right) \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ -4{\alpha }_{1}t & =-4\cdot \frac{1}{4t}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\cdot t \\  & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 5 \\ -4 & -2\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -4{\alpha }_{1}t & -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-4\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(4\text{i}t) & ={e}^{4\text{i}t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}\cdot 4\text{i}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+4{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ 4{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2\cdot \frac{1}{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\cdot t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-\frac{1}{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\cdot t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & 5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues

question.:question/problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ -9 & 4\end{bmatrix}.$ *Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $1,$ and it has multiplicity two.*
${e}^{At}={e}^{t}\,\,$
$1-3t$$t$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ -9 & 4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ -9{\alpha }_{1}t & 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(t) &={e}^{t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(t) &={e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
t{e}^{t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{t}(1-t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-9{\alpha }_{1}t & =-9{e}^{t}t \\ 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4{e}^{t}t+{e}^{t}(1-t) \\  & ={e}^{t}(1+3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}1-3t & t \\ -9t & 1+3t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s))$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}\,x(0) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}+{\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=5x(t)+y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=5y(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}.$*
$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{5}\,\,$
{{field-1}}
$0$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x(0) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{5(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{5(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5t}-\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5t}-\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5t}-\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5t}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Particular Solution of an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs

question.:question/problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 \\ 4 & 2\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}}^{f(t)},\,Φ=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5{e}^{-3t} \\ {e}^{2t} & -4{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix} $$ Consider the system of differential equations and the fundamental matrix of the corresponding homogeneous system above. Using the method of variation of parameters, compute ${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)$ and the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t)$ of the system.
${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)=\,\,$
{{field-1}}
$\frac{3}{5}{e}^{4t}$
$\,,\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)={e}^{t}\,\,$
{{field-2}}

question.:question/worked-solution:
We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5{e}^{-3t} \\ {e}^{2t} & -4{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{0\cdot (-4{e}^{-3t})-5{e}^{-3t}\cdot {e}^{2t}}\begin{bmatrix}-4{e}^{-3t} & -5{e}^{-3t} \\ -{e}^{2t} & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{t}}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-4{e}^{-3t} & -5{e}^{-3t} \\ -{e}^{2t} & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-4{e}^{-2t} & -5{e}^{-2t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{bmatrix} \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-4{e}^{-2t} & -5{e}^{-2t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{22}{5}{e}^{-t} \\ \frac{3}{5}{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}\frac{22}{5}{e}^{-t} \\ \frac{3}{5}{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int \frac{22}{5}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{3}{5}{e}^{4t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{22}{5}{e}^{-t} \\ \frac{3}{20}{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5{e}^{-3t} \\ {e}^{2t} & -4{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{22}{5}{e}^{-t} \\ \frac{3}{20}{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{4}{e}^{t} \\ -5{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{4} \\ -5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Solving an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs Using Variation of Parameters

question.:question/problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 2 \\ -6 & 3\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix}3t \\ t\end{bmatrix} $$ Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form
$x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}+\,\,\frac{1}{9}$
{{field-1}}
$39t+23$
$.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & 3{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}3t \\ t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}\cdot 3{e}^{t}-{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{-3t}}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-2t}}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3t \\ t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4t{e}^{3t} \\ -t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}4t{e}^{3t} \\ -t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int 4t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=4t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=4\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t & =4t\cdot \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\int \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}\cdot (4\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{4}{3}\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t}(3t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=-t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =(-t)\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int (-{e}^{-t})\cdot (-\,\text{d}t) \\  & =t{e}^{-t}-\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{-t}+{e}^{-t} \\  & ={e}^{-t}(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & 3{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t}(3t-1) \\ {e}^{-t}(t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}4(3t-1)+9(t+1) \\ 4(3t-1)+27(t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}21t+5 \\ 39t+23\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$\,\,x(t)+\,\,$

question.:question/worked-solution:
A first-order linear system of differential equations with two dependent variables is a system of equations that takes the following standard form:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=a(t){x}_{1}(t)+b(t){x}_{2}(t)+f(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=c(t){x}_{1}(t)+d(t){x}_{2}(t)+g(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where

- $a(t),$ $b(t),$ $c(t),$ $d(t),$ $f(t),$ and $g(t)$ are known functions, and

- ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are unknown functions (dependent variables).

Such a system can always be written in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

where

$$
x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{bmatrix},\,A=\begin{bmatrix}a(t) & b(t) \\ c(t) & d(t)\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}f(t) \\ g(t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We have the following system.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)+4{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t) &=t \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)-{x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t) &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Writing our system in standard form, we get the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=-4{x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)+t \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &={x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we can rewrite our system in matrix form as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix}t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$
