question.:question/problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.
${({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(5))}^{2}=\,\,$
{{field-1}}$0$$0$$0$
$0${{field-2}}{{field-3}}$1$
$0$$0$$25${{field-4}}
$0$$0$$0${{field-5}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(5))}^{2} & ={\left(\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{1}(3) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{3}(5)\end{bmatrix}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{({J}_{1}(3))}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & {({J}_{3}(5))}^{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={({J}_{1}(3))}^{2}\,⊕\,{({J}_{3}(5))}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{1}(3),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =3.$ since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(3)) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(3)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{3}^{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{3}(5),$ we have $n=3$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first and second derivatives of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{2} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =2x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as 

$$
{J}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-4y+6) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-4y+6) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(xy-2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2xy & {x}^{2}-4 \\ y & x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}2xy & {x}^{2}-4 \\ y & x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}y-4y+6 \\ xy-2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}2xy & {x}^{2}-4 \\ y & x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}y-4y+6 \\ xy-2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2(0)(1) & {0}^{2}-4 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}(0)^{2}(1)-4(1)+6 \\ (0)(1)-2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0 & -4 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get $({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0.5\end{bmatrix}.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0.5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0.5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1.5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}0 & {e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{3t} & -{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{0\cdot (-{e}^{-2t})-{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{3t}}\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{-2t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-{e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{-2t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t} \\ {e}^{2t} & 0\end{bmatrix} \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t} \\ {e}^{2t} & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{-2t} \\ 2{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{-2t} \\ 2{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int 5{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 2{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{2}{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{2}{3}{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & {e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{3t} & -{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{2}{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{2}{3}{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3}{e}^{t} \\ -\frac{19}{6}{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{19}{6}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′} &={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=4{y}^{″}-{t}^{2}{y}^{′}-{e}^{t}y+\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=4{x}_{3}-{t}^{2}{x}_{2}-{e}^{t}{x}_{1}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′} &=-{e}^{t}{x}_{1}-{t}^{2}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -{e}^{t} & -{t}^{2} & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}
$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2(t-1)} & (t-1){e}^{2(t-1)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-1)}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3(t-1){e}^{2(t-1)} \\ 3{e}^{2(t-1)}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2s} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}3(t-1){e}^{2(t-1)} \\ 3{e}^{2(t-1)}\end{bmatrix}+{\int }_{1}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations: $$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}x(t)+{e}^{-5t}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}. $$ The complementary solution to this system is given by $$ {x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}t{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R. $$ Then, the general solution of the system is
$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+$ {{field-1}} $\cdot \,\,$
{{field-2}}
$-1$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
{e}^{-5t}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is exponential. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also exponential, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-5t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $a,b$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=-5{e}^{-5t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5{e}^{-5t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot {e}^{-5t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}+{e}^{-5t}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ -5\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-5a \\ -5b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2a+b \\ 2b\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-5a \\ -5b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2a+b+8 \\ 2b+7\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2a+b+8 &=-5a \\ 2b+7 &=-5b\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get 

$$
2b+7=-5b\,⇒\,b=-1.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation and solving for $a,$ we have

$$
2a+(-1)+8=-5a\,⇒\,a=-1.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-5t}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-3{t}^{2}+4t-4 \\ -{t}^{2}-2t+1\end{bmatrix}
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.

$$

$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{c}_{1},{c}_{2}$ are constants that are to be determined.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\left(\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}{t}^{2}+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\right)+\begin{bmatrix}-3{t}^{2}+4t-4 \\ -{t}^{2}-2t+1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2({a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1})-({a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}) \\ {a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-3{t}^{2}+4t-4 \\ -{t}^{2}-2t+1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}(2{a}_{1}-{a}_{2}-3){t}^{2}+(2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+4)t+(2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}-4) \\ ({a}_{1}-1){t}^{2}+({b}_{1}-2)t+({c}_{1}+1)\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}-{a}_{2}-3 &=0 \\ 2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+4 &=2{a}_{1} \\ 2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}-4 &={b}_{1} \\ {a}_{1}-1 &=0 \\ {b}_{1}-2 &=2{a}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}+1 &={b}_{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the fourth equation and then substituting the corresponding values ​​into the first and fifth equations to solve for ${a}_{2}$ and ${b}_{2},$ we get 

$$
{a}_{1}=1,\,{a}_{2}=-1,\,{b}_{1}=0.

We substitute these into the second equation to solve for ${b}_{2},$ and then into the sixth and third equations to solve for ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ We finally get

$$
{b}_{2}=2,\,{c}_{1}=-1,\,{c}_{2}=-2.

$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Particular Solution of an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations: $$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}. $$ The complementary solution to this system is given by $$ {x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R. $$ Then, the general solution of the system is
$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+$ {{field-1}} $\cdot \,\,$
$-1$
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is exponential. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also exponential, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $a,b$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=-3{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot {e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}+{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\ -3\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-3a \\ -3b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2b \\ 2a\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-3a \\ -3b\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2b+1 \\ 2a+5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2b+1=-3a \\ 2a+5=-3b\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we get 

$$
-2b+1=-3a\,⇒\,a=\frac{2b-1}{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $b,$ we have

$$
2\left(\frac{2b-1}{3}\right)+5=-3b\,⇒\,4b-2+15=-9b\,⇒\,b=-1.
$$

So,

$$
a=\frac{2(-1)-1}{3}=\frac{-2-1}{3}=-1.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{3\times 2}\to R$ defined by $L(A)=\frac{1}{2}(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b),$ where $$ x=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 7\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}? $$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of $L$ with respect to $A$ is a matrix of the same shape as $A$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=Ax-b\in {R}^{3}.$ Then, $L(A)=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{3}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}\left(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y\right)=y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}={y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=Ax-b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}={\sum }_{j=1}^{2}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-{b}_{i},
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}={x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{3}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}{x}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{A}L & =y\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =(Ax-b)\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =\left(\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\left(\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -7 \\ 14\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-10 \\ -5 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -70 \\ 0 & -35 \\ 0 & 63\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-6t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=6t,
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-6t)={e}^{-6t} \\ r(6t)={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t} \\ 6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-12t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t})\right)t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} \\ {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Differentiating the Composition of Vector-Valued Functions

question.:question/problem:
Consider the functions $y:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ and $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{3},$ defined by $$ y(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}^{3} \\ -{x}_{1}{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,f(y)=\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1}-{y}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}^{2} \\ 2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{3}\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))$ evaluated at $$ \displaystyle {x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}? $$
${\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))|}_{{x}_{0}}=\,\,$
$-3$$2$
$0${{field-1}}
{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{3}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{2}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}(2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}(2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{3})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2{y}_{2} \\ 2 & 3{y}_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $$
\displaystyle {y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}0-{1}^{3} \\ -1\cdot 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}-{x}_{1}^{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}-{x}_{1}^{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(-{x}_{1}{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(-{x}_{1}{x}_{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3{x}_{1}^{2} & 1 \\ -{x}_{2} & -{x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $$
\displaystyle {x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \\ -6 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to ${X}_{1}(s)$ and ${X}_{2}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{1}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{2}{s-2}-\frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & =2\,{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-2}\}-{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-4}\}+{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & =2{e}^{2\cdot t}-{e}^{4\cdot t}+1 \\  & =-{e}^{4t}+2{e}^{2t}+1 \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{2}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-4}\}+{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & ={e}^{4\cdot t}+1 \\  & ={e}^{4t}+1\end{aligned}

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{4t}+2{e}^{2t}+1 \\ {e}^{4t}+1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

knowledge_point.title: Applying the Chain Rule to Calculate Gradients

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{2\times 2}\to R$ defined by $L(A)=\frac{1}{2}(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b),$ where $$ x=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}? $$
${∇}_{A}=\,\,$
{{field-1}}$9$
$-6${{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of $L$ with respect to $A$ is a matrix of the same shape as $A$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=Ax-b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}\left(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y\right)=y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}={y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=Ax-b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}={\sum }_{j=1}^{2}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-{b}_{i},
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}={x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}{x}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{A}L & =y\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =(Ax-b)\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =\left(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\left(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & 9 \\ -6 & -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that $$
\displaystyle {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡t & \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.
$$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}\,x(0) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡t & \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}+{\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

$\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2))=\,\,$

$0${{field-3}}{{field-4}}
$0$$0${{field-5}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{2}(2) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{1}(2)\end{bmatrix}\right) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2)) & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{1}(2))\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2))\,⊕\,\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{1}(2)).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{2}(2),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first derivative of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(2)) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{1}(2),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =1.$ \since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(2)) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2))\,⊕\,\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{1}(2)) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing Iterations of the Newton-Raphson Method Using Linear Systems

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0.5,1]\times [1,1.5]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4 \\ x{y}^{3}-2\end{bmatrix}. $$ Fill in the blanks in the matrix equation below that defines the first iteration of the Newton-Raphson process starting at the point $[1,\,1]^{T}.$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
$1$$3$
$({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})\,=$
{{field-3}}
$1$
$.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as

$$
{J}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{3}-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{3}-2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6x & 2y \\ {y}^{3} & 3x{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}6x & 2y \\ {y}^{3} & 3x{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4 \\ x{y}^{3}-2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with $$
\displaystyle {x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},
$$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}6x & 2y \\ {y}^{3} & 3x{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4 \\ x{y}^{3}-1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}6(1) & 2(1) \\ {1}^{3} & 3(1)(1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}3(1)^{2}+(1)^{2}-4 \\ (1)(1)^{3}-2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}6 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-xy-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-xy-4) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(x-{y}^{3}-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x-{y}^{3}-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x-y & -x \\ 1 & -3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}2x-y & -x \\ 1 & -3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}-xy-4 \\ x-{y}^{3}-1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}2x-y & -x \\ 1 & -3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}-xy-4 \\ x-{y}^{3}-1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}2(1)-(-2) & -1 \\ 1 & -3(-2)^{2}\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2}-(1)(-2)-4 \\ 1-(-2)^{3}-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}4 & -1 \\ 1 & -12\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{4\cdot (-12)-(-1)\cdot 1}\begin{bmatrix}-12 & 1 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{47}\begin{bmatrix}20 \\ 33\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{67}{47} \\ -\frac{61}{47}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}1.426 \\ -1.298\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-1) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-3x{y}^{2}-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-3x{y}^{2}-2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x & -2y \\ 3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} & -6xy\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}2x & -2y \\ 3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} & -6xy\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-1 \\ {x}^{3}-3x{y}^{2}-2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}2x & -2y \\ 3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} & -6xy\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-1 \\ {x}^{3}-3x{y}^{2}-2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1.5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}2(-1.5) & -2(1) \\ 3(-1.5)^{2}-3(1)^{2} & -6(-1.5)(1)\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}(-1.5)^{2}-(1)^{2}-1 \\ (-1.5)^{3}-3(-1.5)(1)^{2}-2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1.5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -2 \\ 3.75 & 9\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}0.25 \\ -0.875\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1.5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{(-3)\cdot 9-(-2)\cdot 3.75}\begin{bmatrix}9 & 2 \\ -3.75 & -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0.25 \\ -0.875\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1.5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{19.5}\begin{bmatrix}0.5 \\ 1.6875\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}-1.474 \\ 1.087\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,1]\times [0,1]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=6x{y}^{2}-3{x}^{2}-6xy+2x. $$ Fill in the blanks in the matrix equation below that defines the first iteration of the Newton-Raphson process starting at the point $[0,\,1]^{T},$ and compute the components of the first iteration. Round the answer for ${x}_{1}$ to **three decimal places**.

$6${{field-2}}
$({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})\,=$
$-2$
{{field-3}}

$0$
{{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
{H}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-∇f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(6x{y}^{2}-3{x}^{2}-6xy+2x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(6x{y}^{2}-3{x}^{2}-6xy+2x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2 \\ 12xy-6x\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(12xy-6x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(12xy-6x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 12y-6 \\ 12y-6 & 12x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 12y-6 \\ 12y-6 & 12x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2 \\ 12xy-6x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 12y-6 \\ 12y-6 & 12x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}6{y}^{2}-6x-6y+2 \\ 12xy-6x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-6 & 12(1)-6 \\ 12(1)-6 & 12(0)\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}6(1)^{2}-6(0)-6(1)+2 \\ 12(0)(1)-6(0)\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-6 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get $({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1/3\end{bmatrix}.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0.667\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The Hadamard product of two compatible vectors $u$ and $v$ can be expressed as the matrix product

$$

In our case, we have

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
The second-order differential equation ${y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}-y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ where

question.:question/worked-solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=4{y}^{′}+y+\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=4{x}_{2}+{x}_{1}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, recall the associative law

$$
ABC=(AB)C=A(BC).
$$

Notice that $A$ is a $1\times 2$ matrix, $B$ is a $2\times 1$ matrix, and $C$ is a $1\times 3$ matrix. Therefore, 

- multiplying $A$ by $B$, we will obtain a $1\times 1$ matrix, which will require finding only $1$ entry, while

- multiplying $B$ by $C$, we will obtain a $2\times 3$ matrix, which will require finding $6$ entries.

So, we find the product $AB$ first: 

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 5\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(-1)\cdot 2+5\cdot (-3)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-17\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply $(AB)$ by $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}ABC & =(AB)\,C \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-17\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-68 & 0 & 34\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Differentiating the Composition of Vector-Valued Functions

question.:question/problem:
Consider the functions $y:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{2}$ and $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2},$ defined by $$ y(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2} \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}.\,f(y)=\begin{bmatrix}3{y}_{1} \\ 2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2}\end{bmatrix} $$ What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))$ evaluated at $$ \displaystyle {x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}? $$

{{field-1}}{{field-2}}$0$
$-3${{field-3}}{{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}(3{y}_{1}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}(3{y}_{1}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}(2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}(2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $$
\displaystyle {y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2} \\ 1-(-1)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{3}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}-{x}_{1}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}-{x}_{1}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{2}-{x}_{1})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{1} & 2{x}_{2} & 2{x}_{3} \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 6 & 0 \\ -3 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ $n=2,$ and $\lambda =\frac{\pi }{3}.$

Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first $2-1=1$ derivative of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f\left({J}_{2}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\right) & =\begin{bmatrix}f\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) & {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\ 0 & f\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Applying the Chain Rule to Calculate Gradients

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{2\times 3}\to R$ defined by $L(A)=2(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b),$ where $$ x=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}? $$
${∇}_{A}=\,\,$
{{field-1}}$36${{field-2}}
$72${{field-3}}$180$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of $L$ with respect to $A$ is a matrix of the same shape as $A$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=Ax-b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)=2{y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}(2{y}^{T}y)=4y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}=4{y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=Ax-b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}={\sum }_{j=1}^{3}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-{b}_{i},
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}={x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =4{y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =4{y}_{i}{x}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is $4$ times the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=4y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{A}L & =4y\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =4(Ax-b)\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =4\left(\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =4\left(\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 10\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}36 \\ 36\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}72 & 36 & 180 \\ 72 & 36 & 180\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$
